summary: This StatPearls chapter, authored by Aninda B. Acharya and Juan Carlos Sánchez-Manso and last updated April 24, 2023, describes anosognosia, a neuropsychiatric condition in which a patient is unaware of a deficit or disability. It covers etiology (mainly right parietal lesions, also psychiatric and dementing illness), epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis and evaluation, management, prognosis, complications, and patient education. The chapter notes there is no specific treatment, with vestibular stimulation offering temporary improvement and cognitive therapy helping where the condition persists.
one_line: StatPearls clinical review of anosognosia, a condition where patients are unaware of their own neurological or psychiatric deficits.
key_facts: Anosognosia is a neuropsychiatric condition in which a patient is unaware of an apparent disability or deficit.
Joseph Babinski first described anosognosia in 1914 while highlighting the obliviousness of those with left hemiplegia.
Anosognosia most often precipitates after structural damage from ischemic strokes to the right parietal cortex.
In stroke patients with hemiparesis, the incidence of anosognosia is 10% to 18%.
An estimated 50-90% of patients with schizophrenia and 40% of patients with bipolar disorder demonstrate anosognosia or severe lack of insight.
81% of patients with Alzheimer's dementia appear to have some form of anosognosia, and 60% of patients with mild cognitive impairment appear to have it.
Anosognosia can co-occur with somatosensory neglect (asomatognosia), which also localizes to the right parietal lobe.
The fundamental problem in anosognosia probably relates to an inability of the patient to update their self-image with new information about their deficits.
There is no specific treatment for anosognosia, but vestibular stimulation seems to improve this condition temporarily.
A four-point anosognosia rating scale for dementia ranges from patients who easily admit memory loss to patients who angrily insist no memory problem exists.
Anosognosia differs from denial, a psychological defense mechanism in which the patient may acknowledge a deficit but minimize its consequences.
When anosognosia is due to a focal structural lesion, it typically resolves over time, though it can persist over the long term.
In acute stroke, a patient with anosognosia may not give accurate symptom onset time, so collateral history from a family member is crucial for thrombolytic therapy decisions.
Anosognosia can impair rehabilitation and lead to more frequent falls because patients lack awareness of their deficits.
Egbert AR described an ethical framework for involving patients with anosognosia in their rehabilitation treatment.
